source.title: Machine Learning For Elliptic PDEs: Fast Rate Generalization Bound, Neural Scaling Law and Minimax Optimality
source.authors: Yi-Ping Lu; Haoxuan Chen; Jian-Feng Lu; Le-Xing Ying; J. Blanchet

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figure text are flattened or garbled, but the study and its reported results are identifiable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests power-law scaling in a new setting: Deep Ritz PDE solvers, measuring testing error against training sample count rather than language-model pretraining loss against model, token, or compute scale.
record.gate_note: The paper reports empirical PDE-solver results against training sample count, which bear on V5. Theoretical bounds and scaling-law results cited from other studies are not recorded as findings. No result tests language-model scaling, parameter/token/compute sweeps, compute-optimal allocation, or architecture variation at fixed parameter count.
record.test_reason: Section 6 trains neural Deep Ritz PDE solvers on growing sample counts and fits log-log error-versus-data curves. This is a non-text training regime, so it bears on V5. It tests data-count scaling only.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say their experiments verify their theory and show a dimension-dependent power law (roughly n^(-1/(d+2))) for Deep Ritz solvers, with near-parametric rates for simple targets. Experiments cover DRM only, not PINN. The main contribution is theoretical bounds.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and experiments on Deep Ritz and modified Deep Ritz PDE solvers. Its empirical scaling variable is sampled training data count, and its outcome is PDE-solution testing error, not language-model cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported scaling behavior varies with problem dimension and target function; the paper reports a dimension-dependent law and near-parametric fitted slopes for the two simple-target examples.

fits_no_version.finding: The neural DRM data-scaling exponent shrinks with dimension (inverse exponent roughly linear in d). For simple targets the exponent is near the parametric rate, about 0.5, regardless of d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In non-text neural regimes, the data-scaling exponent depends on the intrinsic dimension and smoothness of the target.

record.problems: Empirical results are limited to Deep Ritz PDE experiments and specified test functions. Figure 2 uses 5 sample-count values and reports medians over 2 replicates; Figure 1 reports medians over 5 replicates. Uncertainty intervals or error bars are not stated, and some plotted results are available only as figure values.

untested.parts: Scaling with model parameters or compute. Only training sample count is varied, over about 2.7 orders of magnitude (20 to 10240 points). Image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. PINN has no experiments.
All parts: no language-model pretraining experiments.
All parts: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All parts: no empirical compute-optimal allocation.
All parts: no shape or architecture variation.
All parts: no language-model fitting-choice analysis.

missing.what: Panel plotting the multiplicative inverse of the fitted scaling coefficient against dimension (4–11), described as highly linear in d. This is the main evidence for the dimension-dependent law.

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence: 5 sample sizes, 2 replicates in Figure 2, and no uncertainty reported. Rows r1–r2 are classical Fourier estimators testing the paper's own theory. The 'tests' relation for V5 is loose: this is a PDE-solver regime with only data scaling, which is not one of the listed V5 examples.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small language-model runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effect of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The experiments are limited to Deep Ritz PDE solvers and the stated test functions; other modalities and regimes, including image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer, are not tested.
Predictability of language-model downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.

Whether language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on parameter counting, training schedule, data, or fitting choices, or whether language-model curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: DRM using Fourier basis
rows.operation_detail: Fit a log-log relationship between H1 loss and number of sampled data points.
rows.measure: Fitted log-log convergence slope for H1 loss versus sampled data count
rows.note: The paper describes a log-log fit and reports the empirical slope and R2 in the figure; the extracted figure text gives R2 = 0.91.
rows.check: The subject is a truncated Fourier-series estimator plugged into the DRM objective, not a neural network. The row tests the paper's own convergence-rate theory (slope 0.6595 vs theoretical 0.75), so it does not bear on V5.

relationships.condition: Neural Deep Ritz PDE solvers, test error vs training sample count (d=5–10, random-NN teacher, simple 10-d polynomial)
relationships.reason: r15 and r16 give near-linear log-log fits (R2 0.96, 0.99). The authors report power-law behaviour in d=5–10 (r3–r8), though those are figure-only with 2 replicates.
relationships.display_finding: Log-log fits achieved R² values of 0.96 and 0.99, and experiments in dimensions 5–10 showed reported power-law behavior with two replicates.
